tagline: Write a poker bot. Submit it. Best bot wins.
intro: Today you write a Python bot that plays heads-up no-limit Texas Hold'em. Your bot only decides what to do each turn; the engine deals the cards and enforces the rules.

When hacking ends you submit your bot as a pickle file plus the Python files it came from, in the submission form. There is one round: every submitted bot plays every other bot, each pairing over many deals with the seats swapped so card luck mostly cancels. The bot with the best score is the champion.

timeline.title: Hacking starts
timeline.detail: Fork the repo on GitHub and clone your fork, set up, write your bot and test it with python -m evals. Run python -m submit --team yourteam early, so you know the process well before the deadline.

timeline.title: Submissions open
timeline.detail: The submission form link appears on this site. Until then submissions are closed.

timeline.title: Submission deadline
timeline.detail: Submissions close. The newest upload that works before 18:00 is the one that plays.

timeline.title: The round
timeline.detail: The organisers read the submitted code, then every bot plays every other bot. The results and replays appear on this site a little behind the real play, and the champion appears with the last match.

rules: One bot per team, submitted with python -m submit as myteam.pkl plus your .py files, in the form that opens at 16:00.
Every move has a time limit of 10 seconds. A crash, a timeout or an illegal move is a fault: the engine checks or folds for you, and a bot that times out is out for the rest of that match.
Keep weights and data inside your model (load them in __init__); files on disk are not available when your bot plays.
Your code is read before it runs. Do not use the network, the file system, or the engine's internals, and do not attack other teams' bots or the organisers' machine.
contact: Stuck? Ask in the WhatsApp group or find an organiser in the room. python -m submit shows what the code review will flag before you upload.
